slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (hematology EDTA tube); heel-stick capillary blood in newborns  ·  Units: %

What it is used for: The count is most often used to diagnose specific types of anemia, see whether anemia treatment is working, check whether the bone marrow makes enough red cells, and check marrow function after chemotherapy or a bone marrow transplant.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: It is ordered when other tests (CBC, hemoglobin, hematocrit) show abnormal red cell levels, during radiation or chemotherapy, after a recent bone marrow transplant and for symptoms of anemia. Newborns may be tested for hemolytic disease of the newborn, which can occur with Rh incompatibility between mother and baby.

Physiology: Reticulocytes are immature (still developing) red blood cells made in the bone marrow; they enter the blood and mature into red cells within one to two days. The count checks whether the marrow makes the right amount of red cells as old ones die off.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Modern analysers do more than count reticulocytes: they measure maturity by RNA content (the fraction of the youngest cells — IRF), cell volume and haemoglobin content (RET-He or CHr). Names, method and reference ranges depend on the analyser.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: Reticulocytosis (a high count) may mean hemolytic anemia (red cells are destroyed faster than the marrow can replace them), new or ongoing bleeding (the body makes many more red cells to replace those lost), or hemolytic disease of the newborn.

A low count may mean iron deficiency anemia, pernicious anemia (a megaloblastic anemia from too little or poorly absorbed vitamin B12 and folate), aplastic anemia (the marrow cannot make enough blood cells), bone marrow failure from infection or cancer, kidney disease or cirrhosis.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: IRF is an early marker of marrow activity: after stem-cell transplantation it shows erythroid recovery before the total reticulocyte count does; Dolgov et al. also cite it as an early sign of response to anaemia treatment.

Reticulocyte haemoglobin content (RET-He, CHr) indirectly reflects the functional iron available for red cell production over the previous 3–4 days; a low value points to iron-restricted erythropoiesis. The cut-off depends on the analyser and laboratory — use the reference on the report.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/7
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed. Adults give a vein sample; in newborns the heel is pricked with a small needle.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/7
bullets: Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/7
bullets: Interferences: Reticulocyte counts may be higher during pregnancy; they rise for a short time after moving to a high altitude and return to normal once the body adjusts. Some medicines may increase or decrease the count.

On analysers reticulocytes can be falsely high because of nucleated red cells (NRBCs), red-cell inclusions or fluorescent interference; with an analyser flag or a result that does not fit the clinical picture, check the smear.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/7
bullets: Limitations: To understand the result, the provider considers symptoms, history and other blood tests; an abnormal count does not always mean anemia or another condition.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 5/7
bullets: In anaemia the absolute count or a haematocrit-corrected index (CRC, RPI) is used instead of the percentage. Takami (2026) gives approximate adult guides: above about 80×10⁹/L suggests an increased marrow response (bleeding, haemolysis, recovery); below about 20×10⁹/L with severe anaemia suggests markedly impaired erythropoiesis. These are not rigid diagnostic cut-offs.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 6/7
bullets: MSCV (mean sphered cell volume) is reported only by some analysers (per the source, Beckman Coulter). In hereditary spherocytosis MSCV is usually lower than MCV, which helps separate it from thalassaemia; the diagnosis is confirmed with the smear, family studies and other tests.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 7/7
bullets: Manual counting uses a supravital stain (e.g., brilliant cresyl blue) and relates reticulocytes to red cells (traditionally per 1000). Since the 1990s automated flow-cytometric counting has replaced microscopy: it is more accurate and precise, but results are not fully standardised between laboratories.

slides.title: Theories of blood formation (as presented by Najmitdinov)
bullets: Unitary theory (Maksimov): all blood cells arise from a single cell — a lymphocyte-like mononuclear cell (lymphoidocyte).

Papenheim, Kryukov, Kassirsky and others: all blood cells arise mainly from one mother cell, the haemohistoblast; it becomes a haemocytoblast, which gives rise to the megakaryocyte (source of platelets), lymphocyte, monocyte, granulocytes (via the myeloblast) and the erythroid series.

Moderate unitary theory: Kryukov and Kassirsky proposed that the monocyte forms directly from the haemohistoblast, bypassing the haemocytoblast, and recommended replacing the unitary theory with this one.

slides.title: Theories of blood formation (as presented by Najmitdinov)
bullets: When vitamin B12 and folic acid are lacking, the haemocytoblast turns into a megaloblast, leading to megalocytes.

Polyphyletic theory (E. Undritz): every cell type has its own precursor — the megakaryocyte from the megakaryoblast, lymphocyte from the lymphoblast, monocyte from the monoblast, eosinophil, basophil and neutrophil from their own blasts, the erythrocyte from the erythroblast.
“Stem cell” theory (Chertkov, Vorobyov): all blood cells derive from a morphologically indistinguishable stem cell. The author of the book (1998) regards it as an unproven hypothesis.

slides.title: The concept of haemopoiesis and haemopoietic organs
bullets: Haemopoiesis is the formation and development of blood cells; embryonic and postembryonic haemopoiesis are distinguished.
Postembryonic haemopoiesis is the physiological renewal of blood cells: new cells are constantly made to replace ageing ones.

The main organs of postembryonic haemopoiesis are the bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen: erythropoiesis, granulocytopoiesis, monocytopoiesis and thrombocytopoiesis take place in the marrow, lymphocytopoiesis in lymph nodes, spleen and thymus.

slides.title: The concept of haemopoiesis and haemopoietic organs
bullets: Haemopoietic tissue is of two kinds: myeloid (bone marrow — granulocytes, platelets, erythrocytes) and lymphoid (spleen, lymph nodes, thymus — lymphocytes).
Red bone marrow makes blood cells, yellow marrow is fatty tissue; red marrow is found in the pelvis, skull, ribs, sternum and vertebrae.
Red marrow takes part in blood formation and immune processes, fighting infection, bone synthesis, and protein, fat, carbohydrate and mineral metabolism.

slides.title: Modern haemopoiesis scheme: the stem cell and cell classes
bullets: By modern ideas all blood cells arise from a pluripotent stem cell; it is morphologically indistinguishable from a lymphocyte and can maintain itself indefinitely (Chertkov and Vorobyov, 1973, as presented by Yusupova).
The stem cell gives rise to the precursors of myelopoiesis and lymphopoiesis, then to unipotent cells of the different lines; morphologically they resemble a blast or a lymphocyte.

Six classes of cells are distinguished in haemopoiesis: stem, semi-stem (partly determined), unipotent, blast, maturing and mature cells; peripheral blood normally contains mainly mature (sixth-class) cells.

slides.title: Modern haemopoiesis scheme: the stem cell and cell classes
bullets: Unipotent cells are sensitive to the poietins of their own line: erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, granulopoietin (leukopoietin), lymphopoietin.

The direction in which a stem cell develops depends on its microenvironment and on substances made in the body; in the thymus, for example, epithelial cells form the microenvironment and make the hormone thymosin.
Najmitdinov (1998) regarded the stem-cell theory as a still unproven hypothesis, whereas the 2022 textbook presents the unitary theory as accepted today.

slides.title: Haemopoietic lines: the sequence of cell maturation
bullets: Erythropoiesis: stem → semi-stem → unipotent (erythropoietin-sensitive) → proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatophilic → oxyphilic erythroblast → reticulocyte → erythrocyte; the cell shrinks, loses its nucleus and accumulates haemoglobin.
Granulocytopoiesis: myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band → segmented granulocyte; at the myelocyte stage cells split into neutrophil, eosinophil and basophil lines.
Thrombocytopoiesis (in the red marrow): megakaryoblast → promegakaryocyte → megakaryocyte → platelet; platelets are shed from the megakaryocyte.

slides.title: Haemopoietic lines: the sequence of cell maturation
bullets: Lymphocytopoiesis: lymphoblast → prolymphocyte → lymphocyte; a marrow stage, antigen-independent (central organs) and antigen-dependent (peripheral lymphoid organs) development.
Monocytopoiesis: monoblast → promonocyte → monocyte; the cell enlarges and the nucleus becomes bean- or horseshoe-shaped.
There is no single accepted nomenclature for the erythroid line; in daily haematology practice Ehrlich’s terminology is widely used.

slides.title: Stages of embryonic haemopoiesis
bullets: The first source of blood cells is the mesenchyme of the yolk-sac wall; primary (megaloblastic) blood formation begins in the first 3 weeks of embryonic life.

After the yolk sac atrophies, the liver becomes the centre of haemopoiesis: secondary erythroblasts, granulocytes and megakaryocytes form from the mesenchyme around liver capillaries; the spleen and lymph nodes join later.
Red bone marrow begins to form in the third month of embryonic life and becomes the main haemopoietic organ in the last month.
T-lymphocytes develop in the thymus, and lymphopoiesis in the spleen and lymph nodes.

slides.title: Stages of embryonic haemopoiesis
bullets: Normoblastic blood formation goes through secondary erythroblasts: polychromatophilic erythroblast → normoblast → secondary erythrocyte (normocyte).

slides.title: What may reticulocytosis indicate, per the source?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the marrow replaces the lost cells.

Basis: A rise — hemolytic anemia or bleeding; a fall — iron deficiency, aplastic anemia and others.

slides.title: What are reticulocytes?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Immature red cells that leave the marrow and mature in 1–2 days.

slides.title: Which parameter shows erythroid recovery earliest after stem-cell transplantation?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: IRF (immature reticulocyte fraction) is an early marker of marrow recovery.

slides.title: Hematopoietic stem cells are characterized by:
Erythropoiesis (normoblastic, megaloblastic). Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the erythroid lineage?
bullets: 1. Erythropoiesis in the bone marrow: hematopoietic stem cell → common myeloid progenitor → erythroid progenitors; the main humoral regulator is erythropoietin, produced in the kidney in response to hypoxia (enhances survival and division of progenitors).

2. Normoblastic (normal) lineage: proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatophilic → orthochromic (oxyphilic) erythroblast → nucleus extruded → reticulocyte → erythrocyte. During maturation the cell becomes smaller, the nucleus condenses, hemoglobin accumulates in the cytoplasm, and basophilia is replaced by oxyphilia.

slides.title: Erythropoiesis (normoblastic, megaloblastic). Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the erythroid lineage?
bullets: 3. The reticulocyte matures in the bone marrow for ~1–3 days and in the blood for ~1–2 days; the mature erythrocyte is an anucleate biconcave disc, circulates for ~120 days and is destroyed by splenic macrophages.
4. Erythrocyte function: transport of O2 and CO2 via hemoglobin; its shape and membrane provide deformability.

5. Megaloblastic erythropoiesis – in B12 or folate deficiency DNA synthesis is impaired: nuclear maturation lags behind the cytoplasm (nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony), the cells are large (megaloblasts), erythropoiesis is ineffective – many cells die in the bone marrow itself.

slides.title: Erythropoiesis (normoblastic, megaloblastic). Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the erythroid lineage?
bullets: 6. In the megaloblastic state, the peripheral blood shows macrocytosis (MCV >100 fL) and hypersegmented neutrophils; in the postnatal period this is always a sign of pathology.

slides.title: Modern theory of blood formation. Regulation of hematopoiesis?
bullets: 1. Modern hierarchical model: self-renewing hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) → multipotent progenitors → common myeloid (erythrocyte, megakaryocyte, granulocyte, monocyte) and common lymphoid (B, T, NK) progenitors → mature cells; newer research shows differentiation as a continuous process.
2. Ontogeny: yolk sac and AGM region → fetal liver and spleen → after birth, bone marrow (and lymph nodes) is the main site of hematopoiesis.

3. Regulation: growth factors and cytokines – erythropoietin (erythropoiesis), interleukins (IL-3, IL-6, IL-7, etc.), colony-stimulating factors (G-CSF, GM-CSF), thrombopoietin (megakaryocytopoiesis).

slides.title: Modern theory of blood formation. Regulation of hematopoiesis?
bullets: 4. Local regulation – the "niche": bone marrow stroma, endothelium and intercellular signals determine HSC quiescence, self-renewal and differentiation.
5. Clinical and laboratory significance: impaired hematopoiesis presents as cytopenias, MDS, leukemias; bone marrow activity is assessed by reticulocytes and bone marrow aspirate.

slides.title: Leukopoiesis. Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the leukocyte lineage?
bullets: 1. Leukopoiesis begins from common myeloid (granulocytes, monocytes) and common lymphoid (B, T, NK) progenitors; regulated by G-CSF, GM-CSF and interleukins.

2. Granulocytic lineage: myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte (neutrophil/eosinophil/basophil direction) → metamyelocyte → band → segmented. During maturation the nucleus condenses and segments; after the primary (azurophilic) granules, specific granules appear.

slides.title: Leukopoiesis. Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the leukocyte lineage?
bullets: 3. Neutrophils – phagocytosis and first defense against bacteria; eosinophils – parasites and allergic reactions; basophils – histamine, allergy; monocytes become macrophages and dendritic cells in tissues.
4. Lymphocytes: B lymphocytes – antibodies (becoming plasma cells), T lymphocytes – cellular immunity and regulation, NK cells – cytotoxicity against virus-infected and tumor cells.
5. Normal values in adults: leukocytes 4.5–11×10⁹/L; neutrophils 40–60%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 2–8%, eosinophils 0–4%, basophils 0.5–1% (varies by laboratory).
